questions.stem: A 34 year old man with HIV, not yet on antiretroviral treatment, has 2 days of central chest pain and breathlessness. He does not smoke. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with non-specific ST changes. Troponin is 2800 ng/L. Coronary angiography shows normal coronary arteries.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Young, few risk factors, HIV, chest pain, tachycardia and a high troponin with normal coronaries is myocarditis; HIV is a recognised clue.

steps.x: **HIV**, young non-smoker, very high troponin, **normal coronaries**.

elim: Tearing pain to the back, BP differential; would not cause this troponin pattern with normal coronaries.
Unlikely with normal coronary arteries in a young non-smoker.
Causes breathlessness and hypoxia, not chest pain with a troponin of 2800.
Can raise troponin modestly, but tachycardia, chest pain and normal coronaries in HIV point to myocarditis.

steps.x: **B. Myocarditis.** Raised troponin + normal coronaries in a young or HIV patient = myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has 3 days of chest pain and palpitations after a week of fever and sore throat. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. A scratchy rub is heard at the left sternal edge. Her echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 42%.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A markedly raised troponin (around 4000) with reduced EF after a viral illness is myocarditis, even with a pericardial rub; isolated pericarditis does not reduce EF.

steps.x: Rub suggests pericardial involvement, but **troponin ~4000** and **low EF** mean the myocardium is inflamed.

elim: Troponin is usually normal or only slightly raised, and EF is preserved.
Expect a new regurgitant murmur and vegetations, not a rub with reduced EF.
Needs Jones criteria (arthritis, chorea, rash, nodules); troponin of 4100 with reduced EF after a viral illness fits myocarditis.
Typically an older woman after emotional stress, with apical ballooning.

steps.x: **C. Myocarditis.** Markedly raised troponin + reduced EF = myocarditis, not just pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has 6 hours of central chest pain 5 days after a cold. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her ECG (see item resources) is shown. She was taken to the cath lab, where coronary angiography is normal. Troponin is 3600 ng/L.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Diffuse ST elevation across several territories with T-wave inversion.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diffuse, non-territorial ST elevation with T inversion after a viral illness, high troponin and normal coronaries is myocarditis mimicking STEMI; there is no role for PCI.

steps.x: STEMI-like ECG, viral prodrome, **normal coronaries**.

elim: Episodic rest pain, often with transient ST elevation in one territory; does not follow a viral illness with diffuse change.
Would be seen on angiography.
Angiography shows no occlusion.
Usually postmenopausal women after stress, with apical ballooning.

steps.x: **B. Myocarditis.** Myocarditis can closely mimic STEMI; normal coronaries + viral prodrome give it away.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has 3 days of chest pain and worsening breathlessness after a flu-like illness. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 88/56 mmHg. His JVP is raised and a third heart sound is heard. Troponin is 5200 ng/L. Echocardiography is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
o: Regional wall motion abnormality in the LAD territory
questions.e: Fulminant myocarditis causes global systolic dysfunction, with ejection fraction often as low as 35%, giving an S3, raised JVP and hypotension.

steps.x: Viral prodrome + **heart failure** + shock = fulminant; whole ventricle inflamed.

elim: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Typical of a coronary occlusion (MI), not diffuse inflammation.
Causes syncope and angina in older patients, with an ejection systolic murmur.

steps.x: **C. Global left ventricular systolic dysfunction.** Myocarditis: global, not regional, dysfunction; EF can fall to 35%.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man is on the cardiac ward with myocarditis diagnosed 2 days ago. He suddenly feels light-headed with palpitations. His pulse rate is 186 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. He is alert. His rhythm strip (see item resources) shows a regular broad complex tachycardia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: Inflamed myocardium is arrhythmogenic: ventricular tachycardia is a dangerous complication of myocarditis and a cause of sudden cardiac death.

steps.x: Regular, **broad** and fast in inflamed myocardium.

elim: Narrow complexes at about 150 bpm.
Slow, not 186 bpm.
Narrow complexes with P waves, and rarely 186 bpm at rest.
Chaotic and pulseless; he is alert with a BP.

steps.x: **E. Ventricular tachycardia.** Myocarditis causes arrhythmias, including VT, and sudden death.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has 1 day of central chest tightness. Her ECG shows ST elevation in several leads and troponin is raised. She is a non-smoker with normal cholesterol and no family history of heart disease. The team is deciding between myocardial infarction and myocarditis.
questions.q: Which additional feature would most support myocarditis?
o: Pain radiating to the left arm
questions.e: Myocarditis often follows a viral prodrome (fever, malaise, URTI) and occurs in young people with few risk factors, which helps separate it from MI.

steps.x: Few risk factors; the best extra clue is a **viral prodrome**.

elim: Occurs in both MI and myocarditis.
Does not distinguish them reliably and is more typical of ischaemia.
Suggests ischaemia rather than myocarditis.
Occurs in both.

steps.x: **A. Flu-like illness 1 week earlier.** Preceding flu-like illness/URTI + atypical demographics = think myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl has a week of fatigue, fever, palpitations and breathlessness on climbing stairs. A fortnight ago she had a cold. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 116 bpm with frequent ectopic beats, and BP 102/64 mmHg. Her troponin is raised and thyroid function and Hb are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, fatigue, palpitations, ectopics and breathlessness with a raised troponin after a cold is myocarditis: inflammation impairs function and causes arrhythmia.

steps.x: Viral prodrome + **arrhythmia** + **raised troponin**.

elim: Does not cause fever or a raised troponin.
Her thyroid function is normal.
Causes fever and fatigue but not palpitations with raised troponin.
Her Hb is normal.

steps.x: **E. Myocarditis.** Myocarditis may present with fatigue, fever and palpitations rather than chest pain.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has 2 days of chest pain after a feverish illness. He is now very breathless lying flat. His pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% on air. He has a gallop rhythm and a raised JVP. Troponin is 6400 ng/L. His chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his lungs?
o: Bronchial breathing at the right base
questions.e: Fulminant myocarditis gives central chest pain after a viral prodrome with overt heart failure: S3 gallop, raised JVP, hypotension and pulmonary oedema with bibasal crackles.

clues: gallop rhythm and a raised JVP
steps.x: Overt **heart failure** in fulminant myocarditis: wet lungs.

elim: Lobar pneumonia; the X-ray shows bilateral oedema.
Pneumothorax.
A large pleural effusion.
Asthma or COPD.

steps.x: **A. Bibasal fine inspiratory crackles.** Fulminant myocarditis = chest pain + viral prodrome + overt heart failure.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman faints at work. A week ago she had a febrile illness with diarrhoea. Her pulse rate is 38 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Troponin is 1900 ng/L and potassium normal. She takes no medication. Her rhythm strip (see item resources) is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her rhythm?
questions.e: Inflammation can involve the conducting system: complete heart block with a raised troponin after a viral illness in a young woman is myocarditis.

steps.x: Young, **viral prodrome**, raised troponin, **heart block**.

elim: She takes no medication.
Her potassium is normal.
Unlikely at 23 with no risk factors after a viral illness.
Does not cause sustained complete heart block or a raised troponin.

steps.x: **D. Myocarditis.** Myocarditis can disrupt conduction, causing heart block.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man collapsed and died while playing football. A week earlier he had a sore throat and fever. At post-mortem his coronary arteries are normal. Histology shows a patchy lymphocytic infiltrate with necrosis of adjacent cardiomyocytes and interstitial oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of death?
questions.e: A lymphocytic (T-cell) infiltrate with myocyte necrosis and oedema after a viral illness is myocarditis, which can cause sudden cardiac death during exercise.

steps.x: **T-lymphocytes** + myocyte necrosis + oedema after a viral illness.

elim: Shows fibro-fatty replacement of the RV, not lymphocytic infiltrate.
Needs a blow to the chest and leaves no inflammation.
Shows myocyte disarray and a thick septum, not inflammation.
His coronary arteries are normal.

steps.x: **E. Myocarditis.** Myocarditis histology: lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man has 2 days of central chest pain and palpitations, a week after a febrile cold. His pulse rate is 114 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes. Bloods are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely blood result?
o: Low TSH with raised free T4
Normal troponin with a raised D-dimer
questions.e: Myocarditis raises troponin, often markedly (around 4000), because inflamed myocytes are necrosing; this is why it mimics MI on bloods.

clues: a week after a febrile cold
steps.x: Myocyte **necrosis** from inflammation releases troponin.

elim: Hyperthyroidism; does not explain chest pain after a viral illness.
Suggests a PE, not inflammatory myocyte injury.
Pancreatitis.
Not a feature of myocarditis.

steps.x: **B. Markedly raised troponin.** Myocarditis: troponin raised, often markedly.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has chest pain and a raised troponin 10 days after a viral illness. His coronary angiogram is normal. A cardiac MRI with gadolinium is requested to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on cardiac MRI?
o: Myocardial oedema with patchy mid-wall enhancement
Normal myocardium with a thickened pericardium only
Septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion
Subendocardial enhancement in the LAD territory
Transmural enhancement in the RCA territory
questions.e: Cardiac MRI is the gold standard: myocarditis shows oedema, hyperaemia and late gadolinium enhancement in a mid-wall or subepicardial pattern, whereas MI is subendocardial or transmural in a coronary territory.

steps.x: Inflammation = **oedema** + **mid-wall/subepicardial** enhancement, not in a coronary territory.

elim: Constrictive pericarditis.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
The pattern of myocardial infarction.
A completed infarct.

steps.x: **A. Myocardial oedema with patchy mid-wall enhancement.** MRI: myocarditis mid-wall/subepicardial; MI subendocardial/transmural.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman arrives in the Emergency Department with chest pain and palpitations 4 days after a sore throat. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% on air. She is alert.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: First-line in suspected myocarditis is an ECG (sinus tachycardia, low voltages, or ST changes mimicking MI) with troponin and echocardiography.

steps.x: Chest pain in ED: **ECG first**.

elim: The gold standard, but not the first test.
Useful later, but the ECG comes first in chest pain.
Not the first step, and coronaries are usually normal.
Reserved for fulminant disease.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** First-line: ECG, troponin, echo; then cardiac MRI.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has chest pain and breathlessness a week after a flu-like illness. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia and troponin is 2300 ng/L. He has bibasal crackles. The team wants to assess his ventricular function at the bedside today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Echocardiography is a first-line test that may show a reduced ejection fraction and global dysfunction in myocarditis.

steps.x: **Bedside** test of LV function.

elim: Assesses coronary anatomy, not ventricular function.
Invasive; for fulminant disease.
Dangerous in active myocarditis.
Looks for coronary ischaemia, not bedside function.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiogram.** Echo in myocarditis may show a reduced ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with suspected fulminant myocarditis is on the intensive care unit receiving inotropes. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg and ejection fraction 25%. She is too unstable to lie in an MRI scanner. Her coronary angiogram is normal. The team needs to know the histological type to guide treatment.
questions.q: Which is the investigation of choice?
questions.e: In fulminant myocarditis, endomyocardial biopsy is the investigation of choice, showing the histological type (for example giant cell or eosinophilic) that changes treatment.

clues: too unstable to lie in an MRI scanner
steps.x: **Fulminant**, unstable, needs histology.

elim: Her coronaries are already known to be normal.
Dangerous and not diagnostic.
Confirms injury but not its type.
Does not prove myocardial involvement or histological type.

steps.x: **B. Endomyocardial biopsy.** Fulminant myocarditis: endomyocardial biopsy.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has myocarditis confirmed on cardiac MRI after a viral illness. He is haemodynamically stable with an ejection fraction of 55% and no arrhythmia on monitoring. His chest pain is mild. He asks what treatment he needs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Uncomplicated myocarditis is managed supportively, with rest and monitoring for arrhythmia and heart failure.

steps.x: Stable, normal EF, no arrhythmia: **supportive**.

elim: For ACS, not inflammatory myocardial injury.
There is no coronary occlusion.
Not indicated in uncomplicated acute myocarditis.
No antiviral therapy is routinely used for viral myocarditis.

steps.x: **E. Rest with cardiac monitoring.** Myocarditis: largely supportive, rest and monitoring.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man was taken for emergency angiography with chest pain, diffuse ST elevation and a troponin of 3900 ng/L after a viral illness. His coronary arteries are completely normal. He is pain free, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Supportive care with monitoring on the cardiac ward
questions.e: Myocarditis is an inflammatory, not occlusive, event: PCI and thrombolysis have no role, and management is supportive with monitoring.

steps.x: STEMI mimic with **normal coronaries**: nothing to open.

elim: There is no coronary disease.
For ACS; there is no plaque event.
There is no occlusion, so PCI has no role.
No thrombus; it only adds bleeding risk.

steps.x: **D. Supportive care with monitoring on the cardiac ward.** PCI has no role in myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with myocarditis has become breathless at rest over 12 hours. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm, BP 108/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on air. She has a raised JVP, bibasal crackles and pitting ankle oedema. Her ejection fraction is 35%.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate drug treatment?
questions.e: Heart failure in myocarditis is treated with standard therapy: diuretics for congestion, then ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker.

clues: raised JVP, bibasal crackles and pitting ankle oedema
steps.x: Fluid overload from **heart failure**: offload first.

elim: Treats SVT, not fluid overload.
No role in myocarditis.
Would worsen pulmonary oedema.
NSAIDs cause fluid retention and are avoided in myocarditis with heart failure.

steps.x: **D. IV furosemide.** Myocarditis heart failure: diuretic, then ACEi and beta-blocker.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with myocarditis on the cardiac ward develops a broad complex tachycardia at 190 bpm. He is confused and clammy with a palpable pulse. His BP is 74/42 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: Arrhythmias in myocarditis are managed by standard ALS guidance: tachycardia with adverse features (shock, confusion) needs synchronised DC cardioversion.

clues: confused and clammy with a palpable pulse
steps.x: VT **with a pulse** and **adverse features**.

elim: For narrow complex SVT; not safe in VT with shock.
Too slow with adverse features; shock first.
Would worsen hypotension and myocardial function.
For pulseless VT or VF; he has a pulse.

steps.x: **D. Synchronised DC cardioversion.** Arrhythmia in myocarditis: treat by ALS algorithms; unstable VT with pulse = synchronised shock.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with myocarditis develops complete heart block. Her pulse rate is 32 bpm, BP 78/46 mmHg and she is drowsy. She has been given atropine 500 micrograms IV twice with no response.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Observe and repeat ECG in 4 hours
questions.e: Heart block in myocarditis is treated by ALS bradycardia guidance: atropine, then pacing (transcutaneous, then transvenous) if there is no response.

clues: atropine 500 micrograms IV twice with no response
steps.x: Unstable bradycardia **unresponsive to atropine**.

elim: Would worsen AV block.
Slows the heart further.
She has adverse features and needs immediate treatment.
For tachyarrhythmias, not bradycardia.

steps.x: **E. Transcutaneous pacing.** Bradycardia algorithm: atropine, then pacing.

questions.stem: A 21 year old university rugby player had myocarditis diagnosed 3 weeks ago. He now feels well, his troponin has normalised and his ejection fraction is 58%. He wants to return to full-contact training next week.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Avoid competitive sport for 3 to 6 months
Return now since troponin has normalised
Return once he has completed 1 week of rest
Return when his chest pain has settled
questions.e: Exercise increases myocardial workload and arrhythmic risk in inflamed myocardium, so competitive sport is restricted (usually 3 to 6 months, with reassessment) to prevent sudden cardiac death.

steps.x: Recent myocarditis + sport: **sudden death** risk.

elim: Restriction is temporary, guided by reassessment.
Normal troponin does not mean the arrhythmic risk has passed.
Far too short.
Symptom resolution does not end the risk.

steps.x: **B. Avoid competitive sport for 3 to 6 months.** Restrict exercise after myocarditis (3 to 6 months) to prevent sudden cardiac death.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man returning from a country with a low vaccination rate has a sore throat with a grey membrane over his tonsils and a 'bull neck'. Ten days later he develops palpitations and breathlessness. His troponin is raised and his ECG shows first-degree heart block. He was never vaccinated.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Coxsackievirus B is the commonest cause of myocarditis, but diphtheria toxin is a recognised cause, after a grey pseudomembranous pharyngitis in an unvaccinated patient.

steps.x: **Grey pseudomembrane** + bull neck + unvaccinated.

elim: Lyme disease, after a tick bite with erythema migrans.
The most common cause overall, but the grey pseudomembrane and bull neck point to diphtheria.
Causes tonsillitis and later rheumatic fever, not a grey adherent membrane.
Chagas disease, from South America, presenting years later.

steps.x: **B. Corynebacterium diphtheriae.** Commonest cause: Coxsackie B; also diphtheria.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has myocarditis 10 days after a viral illness with fever and diarrhoea. Stool PCR identifies an enterovirus. Two weeks later viral RNA is no longer found in her blood, but her troponin is still rising.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of ongoing myocardial injury?
o: Immune complex deposition in the coronary arteries
Ongoing viral replication in the myocardium
questions.e: Cardiotropic enteroviruses such as Coxsackievirus B invade cardiomyocytes directly, followed by a T-cell-mediated immune response against infected and bystander myocytes, which continues injury.

clues: no longer found in her blood
steps.x: Virus clearing but injury continuing: the **immune response**.

elim: Myocarditis is not an occlusive coronary event.
This is diphtheria; she has an enterovirus.
Causes vasculitis, not myocarditis.
The virus is clearing, yet injury continues.

steps.x: **E. T-cell-mediated immune response against cardiomyocytes.** Myocarditis: direct viral invasion, then T-cell-mediated damage.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man had viral myocarditis 3 years ago. He now has progressive exertional breathlessness. His echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30% and global hypokinesia. His coronary arteries are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his heart failure?
o: Myocyte loss with fibrosis and ventricular dilatation
questions.e: Chronic inflammation causes myocyte necrosis and fibrosis, so the ventricle dilates and contracts poorly: dilated cardiomyopathy, a recognised complication of myocarditis.

steps.x: Years after myocarditis + **dilated**, globally weak LV.

elim: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, genetic.
Hypertensive heart disease.
Constrictive pericarditis gives normal-sized ventricles.
His coronaries are normal.

steps.x: **D. Myocyte loss with fibrosis and ventricular dilatation.** Myocarditis can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man has chest pain after a viral illness with a troponin of 4300 ng/L. His coronary angiogram is entirely normal. A student asks how his troponin can be so high if his coronary arteries are open.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Inflammatory injury kills cardiomyocytes, releasing troponin; this mimics MI biochemically even though the coronaries are normal.

steps.x: Troponin = **myocyte death**, whatever the cause.

elim: Does not produce a true troponin of 4300.
His kidneys are not described as impaired, and it would not reach this level.
Raises CK, not cardiac troponin to this degree.
The angiogram is normal.

steps.x: **B. Inflammation causing cardiomyocyte necrosis.** Myocarditis mimics MI because inflamed myocytes release troponin.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with fulminant myocarditis is in the coronary care unit. Her BP is 80/50 mmHg with cold peripheries and a raised JVP. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia and her echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 30% with all segments moving poorly.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypotension?
questions.e: Diffuse myocardial inflammation causes global systolic dysfunction, so cardiac output falls and acute heart failure with cardiogenic shock follows in fulminant disease.

clues: cold peripheries and a raised JVP
ejection fraction of 30% with all segments moving poorly
steps.x: **All segments** weak + cold + high JVP = pump failure.

elim: Peripheries would be warm; the cause is cardiac.
Her JVP is raised.
Hypertrophic or valvular cause; not seen.
Would give regional, not global, hypokinesia.

steps.x: **B. Global reduction in myocardial contractility.** Fulminant myocarditis: global systolic dysfunction causes acute heart failure.

questions.stem: A 19 year old netball player is recovering from myocarditis. Her parents ask why she has been told not to train when she feels well and her ejection fraction is now normal.
questions.q: Which is the main reason exercise is restricted?
o: Exercise raises troponin and confuses follow-up
Exertion directly worsens the T-cell response
Exertion increases arrhythmic risk in inflamed myocardium
questions.e: Exercise increases myocardial workload and arrhythmic risk while the myocardium is inflamed; restriction prevents sudden cardiac death.

steps.x: Normal EF does not remove the **arrhythmia** risk.

elim: Not the reason for restriction.
There is no evidence that exercise reactivates the virus.
Myocarditis is not a coronary disease.
The concern is arrhythmia and sudden death.

steps.x: **E. Exertion increases arrhythmic risk in inflamed myocardium.** Exercise restriction prevents sudden cardiac death from arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has chest pain and a troponin of 1600 ng/L, 8 days after a febrile cold. Her ECG shows T-wave inversion in several leads. Invasive coronary angiography shows unobstructed coronary arteries. She is stable with an ejection fraction of 50%.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Cardiac MRI is the gold standard for myocarditis and the key test separating it from MI when coronaries are unobstructed: mid-wall or subepicardial enhancement rather than a subendocardial coronary-territory pattern.

steps.x: Raised troponin, **normal coronaries**, stable: confirm inflammation non-invasively.

elim: No features favour PE over myocarditis here.
Reserved for fulminant or unexplained severe disease, not a stable patient.
Dangerous in possible myocarditis and not diagnostic.
The coronaries are already shown to be normal.

steps.x: **A. Cardiac MRI with gadolinium.** Cardiac MRI is the gold standard and separates myocarditis from MI.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man is recovering from myocarditis complicated by heart failure. His breathlessness has settled on furosemide and he is euvolaemic. His pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg and potassium 4.4 mmol/L. His ejection fraction is 35%. He has no asthma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment before discharge?
questions.e: Heart failure in myocarditis is treated with standard therapy: an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker (with diuretics), which also helps limit progression to dilated cardiomyopathy.

steps.x: Reduced EF, now euvolaemic: start **prognostic** heart failure drugs.

elim: Antiplatelets are for coronary disease, not myocarditis.
Treatment for pericarditis; NSAIDs worsen heart failure in myocarditis.
No thrombus; no role.
Verapamil is negatively inotropic and worsens heart failure.

steps.x: **C. Ramipril and bisoprolol.** Myocarditis with heart failure: ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + diuretic.
